metadata.section_title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models

text: ## Abstract

[Section: Abstract]
Looped Transformers have recently gained significant attention in machine learning as a powerful attention-based architectural paradigm integrating iterative refinement with recurrent parameter sharing. Variants of this architecture have shown promising results on ARC-AGI and Sudoku, both of which are considered to require multi-step reasoning

[Section: Abstract]
. Looped transformers give rise to recurrent reasoning models (RRMs), such as the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) and the Tiny Recursive Model (TRM). Despite their success, RRMs provide no guarantees of correctness: each iteration predicts a complete problem assignment and greedy decoding can yield constraint-violating solutions

[Section: Abstract]
. In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, 'Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems

[Section: Abstract]
. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers

[Section: Abstract]
. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers

[Section: Abstract]
. Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect

[Section: Abstract]
. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on 9 × 9 Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves 91 . 1% of instances, backtracking accelerates by 33 . 3 × and Glucose 4.1 by 1 . 70 × (median, p < 0 . 001 ), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a 1 . 17 × speedup on perfect-hint 25 × 25 grids

[Section: Abstract]
. 17 × speedup on perfect-hint 25 × 25 grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median 1 . 02 × , n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ( 0 . 90 × ) on 9 × 9

[Section: Abstract]
. 90 × ) on 9 × 9 . These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

[Section: Abstract]

## 1. Introduction

[Section: 1. Introduction]
Looped Transformers/Recurrent Reasoning Models to Solve Combinatorial Problems. Due to their parameter efficiency and inherent capability to execute iterative algorithmic procedures through recursive state updates, looped transformers (Yang et al., 2024) offer a promising framework for solving complex combinatorial problems

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. However, they lack the capacity for rigorous logical verification (Renkhoff et al., 2024), raising the question of how to effectively pair their predictive strength with the exact constraints of symbolic methods

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. At this interface, Recurrent Reasoning Models (RRMs), such as Hierarchical Reasoning Models (HRMs) (Wang et al., 2025) and Tiny Recursive Models (TRMs) (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025), have emerged as specialized looped transformers. Despite being called reasoning models, these models do not alter the inherently inductive nature of machine learning, as they perform no deductive logic

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Rather, they apply a learned operator to iteratively update an internal state. Nevertheless, they exhibit remarkable predictive performance on heavily constrained tasks. This high accuracy is unlocked by a scalable training methodology that leverages intermediate supervision and stop-gradient operations between individual loop iterations to efficiently optimize deeply looped structures

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Consequently, this training paradigm has allowed RRMs to achieve strong empirical results across combinatorial domains, such as Sudoku puzzles and abstract visual reasoning tasks from the ARC-AGI benchmark (Chollet et al., 2025).

[Section: 1. Introduction]
Boolean Satisfiability and Modern SAT Solvers. Combinatorial problems are traditionally encoded as instances of the Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem, the foundational NP-complete problem in theoretical computer science, to provide logical guarantees of cor- rectness

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Over the past decades, practical SAT solving has evolved from a purely theoretical challenge into an industrial-grade methodology driven by various advancements in algorithms, heuristics and data structures that can solve large instances.

[Section: 1. Introduction]
Sudoku as an Established Combinatorial Benchmark. Sudoku puzzles serve as an ideal and widely adopted combinatorial benchmark. Despite their conceptual simplicity, a Sudoku puzzle embodies a rigorous Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) governed by strict, non-local rules

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Given a grid partially filled with digits, the task is to assign symbols to all remaining cells while ensuring that each row, column, and subgrid contains every symbol exactly once. The generalized decision problem is NP-complete (Yato and Seta, 2003), highlighting its intrinsic computational difficulty. Despite its simple rules, Sudoku poses significant challenges for neural networks

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Purely neural approaches often generate locally plausible but globally inconsistent assignments and struggle to extrapolate to unseen grid sizes or symbol sets (Long, 2023; Seely et al., 2025; Giannoulis et al., 2025; Vamsi et al., 2021). Our approach aims to solve this problem by combining neural approaches with exact solvers, which prevents inconsistent assignments and guarantees correctness.

[Section: 1. Introduction]
Neurosymbolic Integration. To formalize the interplay between these empirical neural approximations and exact deductive logic, we contextualize our approach within Kautz's taxonomy of neural-symbolic integration (Kautz, 2022)

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Architecturally, a pipeline that feeds the predictive outputs of a recurrent reasoning model (RRM) into a downstream symbolic SAT solver most closely aligns with a Neuro | Symbolic system (Type 3)

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. While Kautz frames a fully integrated Neuro[Symbolic] architecture (Type 6), where symbolic constraints are natively embedded within the neural execution graph, as the ultimate paradigm for combinatorial reasoning, achieving this state with 100% correctness remains open.

[Section: 1. Introduction]
Existing neuro-symbolic frameworks highlight these limitations when applied to hard constraint tasks. For instance, the neuro-symbolic solver of Hathidara and Pandey (2023) remains restricted to Sudoku puzzles with at most eight missing entries, while oscillatory neural network approaches fail when more than roughly half of the cells are unfilled (Haverkort et al., 2025)

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Even more general neuro-symbolic learning frameworks, such as semantic constraint strengthening, achieve only modest solve rates of around 28% and do not reliably solve full, high-difficulty instances (Ahmed et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019).

[Section: 1. Introduction]
In contrast, recent architectural innovations have closed this empirical performance gap. Recurrent reasoning models have substantially advanced pure neural Sudoku solving, achieving solve rates of roughly 70% on extremely difficult 9 × 9 puzzles with more than half of the digits missing

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Building on this progress, symbol-equivariant RRMs (SE-RRMs) further raise this fully solved rate to over 90%, while remaining exceptionally compact and trainable from small instances (Freinschlag et al., 2026).

[Section: 1. Introduction]
A recurrent reasoning model can propose a full solution to a puzzle in a single forward pass, but it cannot certify it satisfies all constraints. Asymbolic solver offers the counterpart: it guarantees correctness without prior knowledge of promising solutions. Coupling the subsymbolic and symbolic components lets the RRM serve as a prior for the solver's search

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. When the network is correct, the solver verifies an assignment with no extra search; when it is wrong, the solver falls back on its own completeness guarantees and potentially takes advantage of promising subareas of the search space.

[Section: 1. Introduction]
We show that the benefit of this combination is dependent on two factors: (i) the problem's expansive search space dominates the solver's runtime for an instance, and (ii) the ability of the solver to dynamically overwrite its branching choices to exploit the hints of the neural model. Consequently, the accuracy of the hints also determines the benefit.

[Section: 1. Introduction]
Overview. In this work, we introduce Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models (GRRM), a neuro-symbolic framework in which symbolic solvers are guided by the predictive symbol probabilities of a trained Symbol-Equivariant RRM. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the problem setting and defines the search-guidance mechanism for backtracking and CDCL solvers

[Section: 1. Introduction]
. Section 3 presents our experimental evaluation across Sudoku grids of varying sizes, benchmarking G-RRM against naive backtracking and the modern SAT solvers Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0. Section 4 concludes our findings and identifies the conditions under which neural guidance improves solver efficiency. Finally, Section 5 outlines limitations of our work and Section 6 describes future work.
## 2. Problem Setting and Methodological Background

## 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models

We briefly review recurrent reasoning models (RRMs), including HRM (Wang et al., 2025), TRM (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025), and SE-RRM (Freinschlag et al., 2026). Throughout, we follow the notation of Freinschlag et al. (2026). For a more in-depth explanation, please refer to Appendix A.

[Section: 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models]
Problem Setting and Notation. RRMshave been developed for structured problem-solving tasks, such as Sudoku solving or maze navigation, where both the input and the possible solutions consist of assignments of discrete values to grid cells. A task instance is represented as a tuple of discrete symbols X = ( x 1 , . .

[Section: 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models]
. . . , x I ) , x i ∈ Σ , where I is the number of grid cells and Σ is a symbol alphabet with K := | Σ | symbols (e.g., digits and an additional mask symbol). A solution is represented analogously as Y = ( y 1 , . . . , y I ) with y i ∈ Σ .

[Section: 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models]
Operational Principle. RRMs are specialized looped transformer architectures proposed for multi-step reasoning, where the same Transformer-based computational block is repeatedly reused to iteratively refine an internal latent representation (see (2) in Appendix A). As looped transformers, RRMs are highly parameter-efficient due to extensive parameter sharing across recurrent iterations

[Section: 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models]
. Their practical success is largely attributed to a scalable training methodology based on deep supervision and stop-gradient operations. HRM and TRM mainly differ in how they architecturally realize recurrent computation.

[Section: 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models]
Symbol-Equivariant RRMs (SE-RRMs). SE-RRMs modify the standard RRM formulation to achieve symbol equivariance. They introduce an explicit symbol axis into the latent representation, yielding rank-3 tensors of shape D × I × K instead of the standard rank-2 representations of shape D × I , where D is the feature dimension

[Section: 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models]
. This change is reflected in corresponding adaptations of both the input encoding and the recurrent update, in particular through the inclusion of attention over the symbol dimension.

[Section: 2.1. Recurrent Reasoning Models]
SE-RRM provides per-cell symbol distributions that remain meaningful even when the symbol set changes, making it a natural candidate as a learned policy for symbolic search, e.g., for variable ordering in backtracking. This is the key interface for guiding symbolic methods.
## 2.2. Symbolic Search and Verification
## 2.2.1. Backtracking Search

[Section: 2.2. Symbolic Search and Verification]
Backtracking uses depth-first search to explore possible solutions in a search tree while continuously checking constraints and undoing choices when violations occur. For Sudoku, it starts from a partially filled puzzle and repeatedly selects empty cells to fill

[Section: 2.2. Symbolic Search and Verification]
. Nodes in the search tree correspond to partially filled puzzles, while edges represent valid digit assignments to a previously empty cell.

[Section: 2.2. Symbolic Search and Verification]
This strategy guarantees completeness: if a valid Sudoku solution exists, backtracking will eventually find it by systematically exploring all feasible assignments.

[Section: 2.2. Symbolic Search and Verification]
Whenever the algorithm reaches a state in which an empty cell has no valid digit available, the current partial solution cannot be extended to a complete solution. In this case, the algorithm backtracks by undoing the most recent assignment and exploring alternative edges

[Section: 2.2. Symbolic Search and Verification]
. This process is repeated until either a complete valid Sudoku solution is found or all possible assignments have been exhausted.
## 2.2.2. Sudoku as a SAT Problem

[Section: 2.2.2. Sudoku as a SAT Problem]
To solve Sudoku using highly optimized modern SAT solvers, the puzzle must be encoded as a formula in Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF). We introduce Boolean variables x r,c,v indicating that cell ( r, c ) contains value v , where r, c, v ∈ { 1 , . . . , N } for an N × N grid

[Section: 2.2.2. Sudoku as a SAT Problem]
. . . , N } for an N × N grid. Every Sudoku rule constrains a given region (a cell, row, column, or √ N × √ N box) to contain exactly one instance of a value

[Section: 2.2.2. Sudoku as a SAT Problem]
. We enforce this using a standard structural encoding where an At-Least-One (ALO) clause ∨ N v =1 x r,c,v ensures that every cell is assigned at least one digit, while pairwise At-Most-One (AMO) clauses ( ¬ x r,c,v ∨ ¬ x r,c,w ) for v = w forbid duplicate assignments so no cell contains multiple values

[Section: 2.2.2. Sudoku as a SAT Problem]
. This identical ALO/AMO pattern is applied across all rows, columns, and boxes to enforce global constraint satisfaction. Prefilled cells are permanently fixed to true via unit clauses x r,c,v .

[Section: 2.2.2. Sudoku as a SAT Problem]
̸

The resulting CNF formula is satisfiable if and only if a valid Sudoku completion exists. The full encoding requires N 3 variables and yields 11 , 988 base clauses for 9 × 9 , 123 , 904 for 16 × 16 , and 752 , 500 for 25 × 25 grids.
## 2.2.3. SAT Solving

[Section: 2.2.3. SAT Solving]
Modern Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) SAT solvers, like Glucose 4.1 ( glucose4 ) (Audemard and Simon, 2017) and CaDiCaL 3.0.0 ( cadical3) (Biere et al., 2024), evaluate propositional formulas in CNF by combining systematic search with logical deduction and dynamic clause database management

[Section: 2.2.3. SAT Solving]
. Rather than traversing the search space chronologically, a CDCL solver relies on three key foundational features, which we discuss below.

[Section: 2.2.3. SAT Solving]
Heuristic Selection (Variables and Phases). The solver dynamically selects unassigned variables using scoring metrics like Variable State Independent Decaying Sum (VSIDS) (Moskewicz et al., 2001). For each chosen variable, the solver must also select a literal polarity (phase) to determine which truth value to explore first.

[Section: 2.2.3. SAT Solving]
Conflict-Driven Learning and Backjumping. When an assignment triggers a logical contradiction, the solver analyzes the root cause via an implication graph to derive a globally valid learned clause . It then executes a non-chronological backjump to the deepest decision level where the learned clause becomes a unit, permanently pruning the invalid search space.

[Section: 2.2.3. SAT Solving]
Restarts and Database Management. To escape local minima and heavy-tailed runtime distributions, the solver periodically flushes its active assignment stack (the trail) and returns to the root level. Crucially, it preserves its cached variable phases, heuristic scores, and highly active learned clauses during a restart. To prevent memory bloat, it concurrently purges low-utility learned clauses.
## 2.3. G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models

## 2.3.1. General Strategy

We propose G-RRM, a framework that couples recurrent reasoning models with symbolic solvers through search guidance (Figure 1). We instantiate the recurrent model as an SERRM, trained on pairs of partially filled Sudoku grids and their corresponding solutions.

[Section: 2.3.1. General Strategy]
At inference time, SE-RRM assigns a score to each variable-value pair, yielding a matrix ˆ Y ∈ R I × K , where ˆ Y i,d reflects the model's preference for assigning value d to variable i . For each variable i , these scores define a permutation

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

[Section: 2.3.1. General Strategy]
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where arg sort returns indices in ascending order of the scores, i.e., from lowest to highest value. The most preferred value for a variable i is therefore given by the last element of the permutation, d ∗ i = π i ( K ) .

[Section: 2.3.1. General Strategy]
The resulting ordering guides a downstream symbolic solver during search by prioritizing candidate values in decreasing order of their SE-RRM scores, thereby affecting variable selection, branching decisions, or the order of candidate exploration.

[Section: 2.3.1. General Strategy]
When SE-RRM predictions are accurate, the solver can reach a solution with little or no additional search, effectively reducing the process to a sequence of decisions that can be verified efficiently. When predictions are imperfect, they still bias the search towards promising regions of the search space, while the solver explores alternatives as needed.

[Section: 2.3.1. General Strategy]
Importantly, G-RRM does not restrict the search space; it only determines the order of exploration while preserving all feasible assignments. Consequently, correctness and completeness of the underlying symbolic solver remain unchanged, and improvements arise solely from more efficient search ordering.

[Section: 2.3.1. General Strategy]
Because neural guidance influences only the direction of branching decisions, its efficacy depends on both the instance and the solver architecture. G-RRM can yield substantial benefits on search-dominated instances where decision-tree exploration forms the primary bottleneck, such as in backtracking and glucose4

[Section: 2.3.1. General Strategy]
. However, these gains can be masked in solvers with high structural or startup overhead, such as cadical3 , where initial startup costs persist independently of conflict reduction.
## 2.3.2. G-RRM for Backtracking

[Section: 2.3.2. G-RRM for Backtracking]
The efficiency of backtracking strongly depends on the order in which cells and digits are explored. Good exploration directly reduces the size of the search tree and leads to faster solution times. Our approach combines a classical cell-selection heuristic with neural guidance for digit selection

[Section: 2.3.2. G-RRM for Backtracking]
. We use backtracking as the simplest example of G-RRM, making the improvements more pronounced, as the efficiency of backtracking is directly tied to the explored search space.

[Section: 2.3.2. G-RRM for Backtracking]
Cell Selection Heuristic. At each step, the algorithm must choose one of the remaining empty cells. To reduce the size of the search tree, we select the cell with the fewest valid candidate digits. This is the well-known minimum remaining values heuristic and helps expose contradictions early, often reducing the amount of search required to solve the puzzle.

[Section: 2.3.2. G-RRM for Backtracking]
Digit Selection through Neural Guidance. After selecting a cell, the algorithm must decide in which order its valid candidate digits should be explored. Classical backtracking implementations typically use a fixed ordering. Instead, we use the predictions of a trained SE-RRM to guide this decision.
## 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
Neural guidance in CDCL solvers attaches to the phase selection: at each decision point, the solver chooses an unassigned variable together with a polarity (True or False) to try first. This choice determines which region of the search space the solver explores before any conflict is encountered

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
. Correct phase assignment eliminates backtracking entirely; wrong assignment forces the solver to discover and escape an infeasible subspace before recovering. We exploit solver control over this heuristic by initializing phases from SE-RRM predictions before search begins by setting variable phases from the highest-scored digit d ∗ i

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
. The Boolean variable x r i ,c i ,d ∗ i is initialized to 1, and the variables x r i ,c i ,d are initialized as 0 for all d = d ∗ i . Because SE-RRM suggests full solution proposals over all grid cells simultaneously, we map the network's high-confidence predictions directly onto the initial Boolean polarities (phases) of the CNF variables

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
. When the model's hints are highly accurate, the solver can traverse a valid path to the solution with zero or minimal conflicts. The normal configuration omits this step, relying solely on the solver's built-in heuristics.

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
̸

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
̸

We leverage two popular CDCL solvers to evaluate how they interact with this neural phase guidance: glucose4 and cadical3 . Crucially, these solvers manage phase initialization and internal recovery differently when external hints conflict with the underlying logic:

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
- cadical3 : This solver strictly honors externally set literal phases. Provided phases persist across restarts, forcing the solver to consistently prioritize the externally injected search direction unless explicitly overridden by hard learned clause constraints.

[Section: 2.3.3. G-RRM for CDCL SAT Solvers]
- glucose4 : This solver adopts a more fluid approach and may override initial external phases on restart via its native VSIDS-driven reinitialization mechanism. This design yields a significantly faster self-correction loop, allowing the solver to rapidly recover and diverge from faulty hints directing the search into an infeasible subspace.

## 3. Experimental Evaluation

In this section, we evaluate G-RRM by benchmarking different solvers' default configurations against their SE-RRM-guided variants to quantify the impact of neural guidance on solver efficiency for Sudoku puzzles of different sizes. For training details of the SE-RRM, see Appendix B. Additional CP-SAT experiments are located in Appendix C.

[Section: 3. Experimental Evaluation]
Because reduced conflicts directly lead to runtime savings for search-dominated solvers, we quantify the efficiency of G-RRM via changes in conflict counts alongside wall-clock time (see Table 1 and Table 2). In addition, we report the fully-solved rate (FSR), which denotes the fraction of Sudoku instances that SE-RRM immediately predicts correctly, for each benchmarked grid size.

[Section: 3. Experimental Evaluation]
For the SAT solvers, we interface with glucose4 and cadical3 via the PySAT Python library (Ignatiev et al., 2018, 2024), integrating the neural outputs directly into the solver via phase initialization. For the wall-clock time experiments, we separately evaluate the advantage of neural guidance for cases with perfect neural predictions and for cases where the predictions contain errors

[Section: 3. Experimental Evaluation]
. We do not aim to directly compare the performance of backtracking and the CDCL solvers, as we use a custom Python implementation of backtracking. Rather, we compare the normal and guided version of each solver.
